name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,304

clue.text: Least expensive copy found in wooden box (8)

indicators.note: the copy is found inside the box, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a chest is a wooden box

annotation.surface: A bargain hunter finds the cheapest replica packed in a wooden crate.
annotation.walkthrough: Copy reads as a noun, a replica sitting in the box, but it is the verb: to copy someone is to imitate them.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the cheapest item is the one that costs least, the superlative of cheap.

clue.text: Swimmer ultimately broke cipher (4)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the last letter

blocks.note: a cod is a fish, a swimmer

annotation.surface: A swimmer finally cracks a secret code.
annotation.walkthrough: Swimmer is a crossword favourite for a fish; broke looks like the verb for cracking a cipher but only supplies its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a cipher is a system for disguising messages, which is one sense of code.

clue.text: Gale disturbed European bird (5)

indicators.note: disturbed letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European

annotation.surface: A storm unsettles a bird flying over Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: Only GALE is rearranged; the E for European is tacked on after it.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the great raptor on many national emblems is named only by its broad class.

clue.text: Aviation enthusiast quietly tracks ceramicist (12)

blocks.note: lanes are tracks, as on a running track

annotation.surface: A plane buff silently follows a pottery maker around.
annotation.walkthrough: Tracks reads as a verb (follows) but is the noun, lanes.
annotation.definitionFit: A planespotter is a hobbyist who watches aircraft and logs their registrations, so an enthusiast for aviation.

clue.text: Choose the Spanish to infiltrate faction (6)

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside, so EL goes within SECT

annotation.surface: An order to pick the Spanish team to infiltrate a rival group.
annotation.walkthrough: The Spanish is a crossword staple for the Spanish article; the faction is the outer word, not a group being joined.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: you select a card from the pack exactly as you choose one.

clue.text: Some nap secretly in part of church (4)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of nap and the start of secretly

annotation.surface: Someone sneaks a nap in a quiet corner of the church.
annotation.walkthrough: Secretly suggests hiding but only supplies letters: n-AP SE-cretly spells the answer across the word break.
annotation.definitionFit: The apse is the rounded or vaulted recess at the east end of a church, usually behind the altar.

clue.text: Musician heading back inside west Sinai peninsula (7)

indicators.note: heading back means going in the opposite direction, so read the letters right to left
the answer lies inside the following words

annotation.surface: A musician trekking home through the western Sinai.
annotation.walkthrough: The geography is pure scenery: the musician is spelt backwards across west, Sinai and peninsula.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: someone who plays the piano is one kind of musician.

clue.text: Jeopardise finale and get cross (8)

blocks.note: to anger is to make cross; here, grow cross

annotation.surface: Spoiling the last act of a show and then losing your temper about it.
annotation.walkthrough: Anger is loosely clued as get cross; the two pieces simply join.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to put something in danger is to jeopardise it, and danger sits visibly inside the answer.

clue.text: Peer group? (5,2,5)

blocks.note: read as an equal, someone of your own age or standing, and meant as a British noble with a title
on the surface your circle of friends; in the answer the chamber where those nobles sit together

annotation.surface: A phrase for people of your own age and standing.
annotation.walkthrough: A peer group usually means your equals, but a peer is also a British noble, and the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: The upper chamber of the UK Parliament is made up of peers, so it is the peers' group in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Closely follow mum’s doctrine (5)

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
ma is mum; the apostrophe s joins it to the definition

annotation.surface: Advice to stick close to your mother's teachings.
annotation.walkthrough: Mum's reads as possessive but works as mum is: MA followed by the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a dogma is a set of beliefs laid down as beyond question, as a church's doctrine is.

clue.text: American writer turned into fat cat (7)

indicators.note: turned means turned around, so the writer's name runs backwards
the reversed name goes into the fat

blocks.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer

annotation.surface: An American author has been transformed into a fat cat, a wealthy bigwig.
annotation.walkthrough: Fat cat looks like one phrase for a rich person; split it, and fat is the container while cat alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the spotted hunter of Africa and Asia is one of the big cats.

clue.text: Consequence of extremely rude orchestra section (12)

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the first and last letters

blocks.note: the percussion is a section of the orchestra

annotation.surface: The fallout from a very rude drum section in an orchestra.
annotation.walkthrough: Extremely rude reads as very rude, but extremely only asks for the ends of rude.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for an effect that rebounds on you, the word originally meaning an echo or recoil.

clue.text: Cooked canapé with US kitchen utensil (8)

indicators.note: cooked letters are worked into a new form

annotation.surface: A canapé prepared with an American kitchen gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: US looks like the abbreviation for American, but it is just two more letters for the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the long-handled pan for boiling and sauces is one of the basic tools of any kitchen.

clue.text: Tolerate part of play featuring creep periodically (6)

indicators.note: featuring means including, so the part of the play holds the other letters
periodically means at regular intervals, so take every other letter

blocks.note: an act is part of a play
C-r-E-e-P, the first, third and fifth letters

annotation.surface: Putting up with a scene in a play in which some creep keeps appearing.
annotation.walkthrough: Creep looks like the villain of the scene; periodically asks only for its odd letters, which slot into the part of the play.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to put up with something, as in accepting a situation you cannot change.

clue.text: Mysterious wail before photo capturing ghost’s foot (7)

indicators.note: capturing means holding inside, so the photo holds the letter
the foot of a down word is its bottom, the last letter

blocks.note: pic is short for picture, a photo

annotation.surface: An eerie wail heard just before a photo catches a ghost's foot.
annotation.walkthrough: Foot is the crossword way to say last letter, a word's bottom; the ghost itself contributes a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: something cryptic is puzzling or hard to fathom, which is why these crosswords carry the name.

clue.text: Detest a hotel terribly (6)

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters are badly jumbled

annotation.surface: A guest who really hates their hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: Terribly reads as an intensifier for detest but is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, both verbs naming the strongest kind of dislike, well beyond merely not liking something.

clue.text: Rather drunk, beginning to bet on numbers game (6)

indicators.note: the beginning of bet is its first letter

blocks.note: lotto is a lottery or bingo-style game of numbers

annotation.surface: A tipsy gambler starts placing bets on a lottery.
annotation.walkthrough: Rather is British understatement here, meaning very rather than somewhat.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: someone blotto has drunk so much they can barely stand.

clue.text: Scarlet Lycra pants very obvious! (7,5)

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are made a mess of

annotation.surface: Red stretchy trousers leave nothing to the imagination.
annotation.walkthrough: Pants looks like a noun for trousers; in British slang it also means rubbish, a fair sign to scramble.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: something as clear as crystal hides nothing, so anyone can see it.

clue.text: More unhappy after losing small snake (5)

indicators.note: the word loses a letter, so remove it

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, which is removed

annotation.surface: Someone grows gloomier after losing a small pet snake.
annotation.walkthrough: Small looks like it describes the snake, but it is the letter dropped from the front of the longer word.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the venomous viper common across Europe is one kind of snake.

clue.text: Wisecrack from judge offended King Edward primarily (4)

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so take each first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the four words

annotation.surface: A judge's quip has insulted King Edward.
annotation.walkthrough: The royal scene is scenery; only the initials matter.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a wisecrack is a quick witty remark, which is a kind of joke.

clue.text: Inventor’s right to hug one invalid? (7)

indicators.note: to hug is to hold close, so the right wraps round one

blocks.note: a patent is an inventor's legal right
I is the Roman numeral one

annotation.surface: Is an inventor's right to embrace someone void?
annotation.walkthrough: Invalid reads as the adjective, not valid; it is the noun, a sick person.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an invalid is someone laid up by illness, the kind of person a doctor treats as a patient.

clue.text: Wireless advertisement in Brazilian city (5)

indicators.note: the advertisement goes in the city

annotation.surface: A radio commercial playing in Rio.
annotation.walkthrough: Wireless is an old British word for a radio set, from the days before it was a word for Wi-Fi.
annotation.definitionFit: Dated British use: the wireless was the household radio set.

clue.text: Pleasant afternoon finally to chill (4)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so take the last letter

annotation.surface: A pleasant afternoon when you can at last relax.
annotation.walkthrough: Chill suggests relaxing, but here it means to cool something down.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a nice day is a pleasant one, the everyday sense of the word.

clue.text: Save prisoner to join the military? (8)

blocks.note: a con is a convict, a prisoner
to serve is to be in the armed forces

annotation.surface: Rescue a convict so they can enlist in the army.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that join the military is a loose, playful way to describe signing up for service.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to conserve energy or water is to save it by not wasting it.
